key_claim: Compounding means returns earn returns, so most long-term growth comes late, and fees compound against you too.

slides.headline: Returns earn returns
slides.body: At 7% a year, $10,000 grows to about $19,700 in 10 years. After that it speeds up, because each year builds on a bigger pile.

slides.headline: Fees compound too, against you
slides.body: On $100,000 over 30 years, a 2% yearly fee instead of 0.2% can cost you over $200,000.

slides.headline: A few points, a huge gap
slides.body: Over 30 years, 7% a year ends with more than double what 4% does.

caption:
The same $10,000 can become $32,000 or $76,000.

Returns earn returns: at 7% a year, $10,000 grows to about $19,700 in 10 years, then speeds up.

The catch? Fees compound too. On $100,000 over 30 years, a 2% yearly fee instead of 0.2% can cost over $200,000.

The payoff: over 30 years, 7% a year ends with more than double what 4% does.

Illustrative numbers, before fees and taxes. Not financial advice.

Source: Waypoint — Compounding and Index Funds
